memory_candidates.content: When a task's design report names a specific file as the site for a behavioral change, verify by grep that the file is actually in the target command's call graph BEFORE planning against it. Concrete instance: orchestrator-postflight.sh's Stage 7a increments next_artifact_number and its header describes a shared research/plan/implement postflight, but it is called only from skill-implementer/SKILL.md (plain /implement). skill-orchestrate/SKILL.md never calls it. /orchestrate's real postflight path is orchestrate-stage5-postflight.sh (single-task, Stage 5's 'Shared postflight tail') and Stage MT-4 (multi-task), both converging on skill_postflight_update/skill_link_artifacts in skill-base.sh. Editing the wrongly-named file would pass a superficial review -- the named file did change in the way described -- while changing nothing about the intended command's behavior. The general lesson: a plan that inherits a target-file name from a design report should treat that name as a hypothesis, and the grep confirming it is cheap.

Pattern for planning a change to a file that concurrent sibling tasks also edit: partition by POSITIONAL SLOT and by STAGE/REGION rather than by file. Concrete instance from skill-base.sh's skill_postflight_update (signature: 1 task_number, 2 operation, 3 session_id, 4 status, 5 phase_check_mode): one task claims positional 6, another claims positional 7 and adds ONLY its own `local x="${7:-}"` line, never reading or renumbering 6. A positional gap is harmless in bash regardless of landing order, so the two changes compose without a merge conflict and without an ordering dependency. The same partitioning works for a large prose SKILL.md: assign each concurrent task its own new stage heading plus append-only bullets in shared lists, and have it reference sibling-owned handler bodies by heading pointer rather than editing them. Referencing a sibling-owned section is not a collision; only editing it is.

Deploy-first dependency resolution silently invalidates tests for source-store-only edits. In a repo where .claude/ is a gitignored deploy artifact regenerated from agent-system/extensions/**, most loaders resolve deploy-tree-first with a source-store fallback: test-skill-base-lifecycle.sh and test-status-vocabulary.sh both try $REPO_ROOT/.claude/... before $SCRIPT_DIR/..; update-task-status.sh does the same for its lib; skill-base.sh sources lib/common.sh via ${SKILL_REPO_ROOT}/.claude/ first; and orchestrate-stage5-postflight.sh sources skill-base.sh cwd-relative from .claude/ first. Because the deployed copy always exists, editing only the source store means every one of these keeps loading the OLD code -- a new test then fails spuriously or, worse, passes while exercising nothing. Critically this is a CHAIN: sourcing the source-store entry point is not enough, because its own internal sources resolve deploy-first too, so a partial fix yields 'command not found' on the new function rather than a clean signal. The fix is a scratchpad harness carrying source-store copies of every edited file (not just the entry point) plus deployed copies of everything else. Two anti-patterns to refuse: deploying in order to make a test pass (destroys the signal the test exists to give, and regeneration is a manual user-owned operation), and reordering an existing suite's resolution (the deploy-first order is deliberate -- the deployed tree is what actually runs). Note the order is not even uniform: generate-todo.sh and validate-state.sh resolve SCRIPT_DIR-first, so never assume a direction without checking the specific loader.
